claims.text: HEA nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
Structural and chemical stability over 473–1923 K is governed by the interplay of configurational entropy and lattice-distortion effects.
At high temperatures, configurational entropy stabilizes chemically disordered solid solutions over ordered intermetallic or segregated phases.
At lower temperatures, ordering enthalpy can overcome entropic stabilization.
Lower-temperature or extended reactive operation can produce elemental clustering or incipient phase separation.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneous, chemically random solid solutions with uniformly distributed constituent metals.
Differences in constituent atomic sizes produce significant lattice distortion in HEAs.
Lattice distortion reduces or modulates atomic diffusion kinetics.
Lattice distortion modulates local bonding environments.
If diffusion kinetics permit, thermodynamically favorable ordering can produce local clustering or secondary phases.
The nanoparticles will retain a uniform single phase at high temperatures throughout the specified operating conditions.
HEA nanoparticles can retain structurally similar, well-mixed states between 573 and 1000 K.
Reactive species can induce surface compositional changes relative to the initial homogeneous state.
The as-synthesized nanoparticles have minimal lattice defects beyond inherent lattice distortion.
The proposed stability behavior holds only when no element or metal pair has a dominant ordering enthalpy or extreme diffusion behavior.
Strong chemical ordering between particular metal pairs can cause a different stability mechanism.
An operating environment that accelerates metal leaching can cause a different stability mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says limited diffusion kinetics can lead to clustering, while the mediator and mechanism imply that reduced diffusion inhibits rearrangement and that clustering occurs only if diffusion kinetics permit it.

The prediction expects segregation or clustering during prolonged low-temperature or reactive operation, but the falsification rule broadly treats significant segregation or clustering as falsifying without restricting that criterion decisively to the high-temperature regime.
